| [LIT-226](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-226.md) v2 | The Conditional Entropy Bottleneck | Fischer (2020), [ARXIV-2002.05379](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.05379). The Conditional Entropy Bottleneck minimizes I(X;Z\|Y) − γI(Y;Z), which is the Information Bottleneck with γ = β − 1, aimed at the "Minimum Necessary Information" point I(X;Y) = I(X;Z) = I(Y;Z). On Fashion MNIST it improves accuracy, adversarial robustness, OoD detection and calibration over VIB and deterministic baselines, and it does not memorize random labels. On CIFAR-10 it improves accuracy and robustness. That excess retained information causes these failures is stated as a hypothesis and supported only empirically. | Active — read 2026-10-14 (NOTE-754) in full; worth reading as the paper that names the Minimum Necessary Information point I(X;Y) = I(X;Z) = I(Y;Z), shows that its objective is the Information Bottleneck with γ = β − 1, and gives variational bounds (the residual information ReX) that make the distance to that point observable. Its CatGen decoder is InfoNCE with the backward encoder as critic, capped by log K. Read it knowing that the causal claim, that retained information causes adversarial vulnerability, miscalibration, poor OoD detection and memorisation, is a hypothesis supported only by Fashion MNIST and one selected CIFAR-10 model per setting, and that the arXiv v1 prints the CatGen inequality (Eq. 30) with the wrong sign. |

The NT-Logistic and spectral losses are minimized over unconstrained kernels by K⁺ = p⁺/(p⊗p), and InfoNCE by K⁺ up to a constant per communicating class (over symmetric functions, with the minimizer form taken from Van den Oord et al.). Kernel PCA under K⁺ returns λ_i^(1/2) times the positive-pair chain's eigenfunctions (Thm 3.2). The top-d span minimizes worst-case L²(p) error over approximately view-invariant targets, at ε/(2(1 − λ_(d+1))), provided d is at least the number of communicating classes (Thm 4.1). Read it knowing that everything is proved on finite spaces at the unconstrained population optimum. The supporting experiments are synthetic, and the authors report that they could not extract the eigenfunctions from real-data models. |
| [LIT-267](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-267.md) v3 | The Lattice Representation Hypothesis of Large Language Models | Xiong (2026), [ARXIV-2603.01227](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.01227). Thresholding linear attribute directions (Fisher-LDA probes) gives a crisp object–attribute incidence, and the paper's Theorem 1 is the standard fact that any such incidence has a complete concept lattice. The geometric meet is half-space intersection; the join is defined as the set union of two cones and "approximated by the conic hull" of their directions, which as written is not a lattice join. On five WordNet domains with GPT-4o-annotated attributes, the probes recover the incidence at F1 69.7–83.2 on three 7–8B models, and profile-based subsumption reaches F1 57.1–77.1. No lattice law is ever tested. | Proposed — read in full 2026-09-27 (NOTE-240); promising as a bridge between probe geometry and formal concept analysis, and unproven as a hypothesis about LLMs. It would be settled by three things. The attributes would have to come from something other than another LLM's annotations. The region-level join would have to be defined correctly, as the Galois closure of the shared intent. And lattice identities (closure, absorption, meet/join agreement with the recovered context) would have to be tested, not pairwise subsumption and candidate ranking alone. |
| [LIT-269](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-269.md) v2 | Attention Approximates Sparse Distributed Memory | Bricken & Pehlevan (2021), [ARXIV-2111.05498](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.05498). Kanerva's SDM read weights each stored pointer by the number of neurons in the intersection of two Hamming balls of radius d. The paper shows that this weight is roughly log-linear in Hamming distance for close patterns. As a result, with L²-normalised vectors and a regression-fitted β, softmax attention reproduces SDM's retrieval behaviour on random and learnt-projection data (App. B.7). Two things are weaker than they look. The analytic derivation (App. B.2, Eqs. 16–21) gets the exponent wrong: by my recomputation its β is ≈2–2.5× too small. The biological case is Kanerva's 1988 cerebellar mapping, restated rather than re-argued. It also needs r = 2⁶⁴ ≈ 1.8×10¹⁹ neurons in the Attention setting, which the paper itself calls "biologically implausible" (App. B.5). | Active — read in full 2026-09-27 (NOTE-242); worth reading as the clearest statement of the SDM–attention correspondence. Its exact circle-intersection formula and its eight-algorithm convergence comparison are the parts to take away. Treat its analytic exponential derivation, its GPT-2 "confirmation" and its cerebellar implementation of attention as argument, not demonstration. |

It then uses the basis-copying map σ: v_i ↦ v_i⊗v_i of the Frobenius algebra fixed by W's basis to lift corpus-built verb matrices Σ_i sbj_i⊗obj_i into rank-3 tensors. So a transitive sentence becomes sbj⊙(verb·obj) ("copy-subject") or obj⊙(verbᵀ·sbj) ("copy-object"), a vector in W. On the Grefenstette–Sadrzadeh verb-disambiguation set, copy-object gets Spearman ρ=0.172, against 0.168 (Kron), 0.163 (Multp), 0.143 (copy-subject), 0.050 (additive) and an inter-annotator bound of 0.620. On a 112-term definition-matching task the best F1 is 0.21 (nouns) and 0.27 (verbs). No significance test is reported. The disambiguation numbers are identical to the authors' COLING 2012 paper, and the definition numbers are the same data re-reported. | Active — read in full 2026-09-27 ([NOTE-246](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-246.md)); worth reading for the construction, not for its evidence. Its experiments are the authors' COLING 2012 numbers, re-reported without that paper's caveat that copy-object's lead is statistically insignificant. The best disambiguation ρ is 0.172, against a human bound of 0.620. The construction depends on a choice of basis, which the paper cites but never draws the consequence of. |

A position paper with one argument and three measurements. Measured with mutual 10-nearest-neighbour overlap, vision models that solve more VTAB tasks agree more with each other (78 models). Language models with lower bits-per-byte agree more with DINOv2, CLIP and others on Wikipedia image–caption pairs, and this alignment tracks HellaSwag and GSM8K scores. The cross-modal score "only reaches 0.16" out of a maximum of 1 (§6), and a CKA version "revealed a very weak trend" (App. A). The formal argument (§4.2, App. F) shows only this: in an idealised world of discrete events seen through bijective observations, the Bayes-optimal NCE critic is the pointwise-mutual-information kernel plus a constant, and that kernel is representable as an inner product under a sufficient smoothness condition (Prop. F.1). So every such modality shares one kernel, up to an additive constant. | Active — read in full 2026-09-29 (NOTE-286); worth reading as the source of the "Platonic representation hypothesis" and of the one clean formal statement behind it (Bayes-optimal NCE critics equal the PMI kernel, so bijective modalities share a kernel). Read the empirical case as local nearest-neighbour agreement of modest size, chosen after CKA showed little. | [LIT-304](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-304.md) v2 | The Linear Representation Hypothesis and the Geometry of Large Language Models | Park et al. (2023), [ARXIV-2311.03658](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03658). Three readings of "concepts are directions" are made precise with counterfactual pairs, and proved to line up. The shared direction of word-pair differences in the unembedding space is a logit-linear probe (Thm 2.2). The embedding-space direction is a steering vector that leaves causally separable concepts unchanged (Thm 2.5). Under any inner product making separable concepts orthogonal, the Riesz map sends the first to the second (Thm 3.2). Softmax training fixes the representation only up to γ ↦ Aγ + β, λ ↦ A⁻ᵀλ, so no inner product is identified, and the paper chooses M = Cov(γ)⁻¹ by setting a free diagonal D to the identity (Thm 3.4). Evidence: 27 concepts on LLaMA-2 7B (26 show a common direction; thing⇒part does not), read from histograms and heatmaps with no test statistic, plus a Gemma-2B heatmap comparison. | Active — read in full 2026-09-29 (NOTE-302); worth reading as the short, precise source of the counterfactual-pair formalisation of the linear representation hypothesis and of the observation that softmax training leaves the representation's inner product unidentified. Read its theorems as statements about the final-layer context vector and the unembedding only. Read the choice M = Cov(γ)⁻¹ as a stipulation (D = I), not as a result, and the experiments as qualitative. |

The "if" direction is a short coset computation. The "only if" direction goes through the group Fourier transform: equivariant maps preserve isotypic components (Lemma 6) and act on each Fourier matrix by right multiplication, M ↦ MB (Lemma 10), which the convolution theorem (Prop. 2) turns back into a convolution. | Active — read in full 2026-09-29 (NOTE-282); worth reading as the standard ML statement of "equivariance ⇔ convolution" for compact groups and as a compact introduction to isotypic decomposition and noncommutative Fourier analysis for neural networks. Read the "only if" proof as an outline. It is written out for finite or countable groups and scalar channels only, and one step (removing the pointwise nonlinearity) does not hold as stated for ReLU. |

| [LIT-323](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-323.md) v2 | Toy Models of Superposition | Elhage et al. (2022), [ARXIV-2209.10652](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.10652). In a toy autoencoder x′ = ReLU(WᵀWx + b), with n sparse synthetic features compressed into m < n dimensions, a linear model keeps only the top-m features, but with the output ReLU and sparse enough features the model stores more features than dimensions ("superposition"), in non-orthogonal directions whose interference the ReLU and a negative bias filter out. Whether a feature is dropped, superposed or given a dedicated dimension changes discontinuously with sparsity and importance, and in the n = 2, m = 1 theory this is a first-order phase change. With uniform features the directions settle into uniform polytopes, with feature dimensionalities clustering at 3/4, 2/3, 1/2, 2/5 and 3/8. A ReLU hidden layer creates a privileged basis in which monosemantic and polysemantic neurons coexist, and a model can compute \|x\| for more features than it has neurons. Everything is shown in toy models only, and the authors expect the geometry and learning-dynamics results to generalise least. | Active — read in full 2026-09-29 (NOTE-278); worth reading as the founding statement of the superposition hypothesis and of the vocabulary the field now uses: features as directions, privileged versus non-privileged bases, polysemanticity as interference, and feature dimensionality. It is also the cleanest demonstration that a nonlinearity plus sparsity makes it optimal to store more features than dimensions. Its evidence is toy models alone, which the paper says plainly. Its phase-change and polytope results are exact only for n = 2, m = 1 and uniform features. |

It reports two phases: a short "ERM" phase of a few hundred epochs in which I(T;Y) rises, and a long "compression" phase in which I(X;T) falls. For a real n×N matrix a, the rank-r matrix β nearest in the least-squares (Frobenius) distance is obtained by writing a = u′λU (u, U orthogonal, λ diagonal ≥ 0, "Theorem I") and zeroing all but the r largest diagonal elements. The solution is unique unless λ_r = λ_{r+1}. The squared error is Σ_{i>r} λ_i², so the error is at most l(1−r/R)^{1/2}, with l the length of a and R its rank. The paper also argues that the resulting canonic components cannot straightforwardly be read as psychological factors. | Active — read in full 2026-09-29 ([NOTE-301](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-301.md)); worth reading as the short, readable origin of the Frobenius-norm low-rank approximation theorem in the form still used. There are no experiments.' | Proposed — re-read jointly with [LIT-373](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-373.md) and arXiv 2602.07974 on 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-322](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-322.md)); promising and unproven. Read jointly with the companion arXiv 2602.07974, which carries the fuller statements and several definitions this paper leaves implicit. The formal core holds in repaired form: width as a structural complexity incomparable with the per-cell VC dimension; an error floor below width; the Ω(w log w) discovery cost; an additive Rademacher bound for routed predictors. The flagged slips are repairable and not load-bearing: the bouquet cover, the non-degeneracy assumption in the appendix, Massart, and pseudo-dimension against fat-shattering in Thm 4.6. What remains unproven are the claims that would make it matter: that the CS estimator converges to width itself and not to a predictor-relative count; that a monolithic model cannot match K ≥ w routing; above all, that router/scaffold training should be decoupled from task loss. This is presented as derived from the additive bound, but the bound holds for joint training too. The alignment section is asserted. What would settle it: on synthetic benchmarks of known width, (i) a K-sweep showing the floor at K < w for routed learners and its absence or presence for capacity-matched monolithic models; (ii) CS width recovery from a cold start; (iii) decoupled against joint router training, compared on forgetting and boundary error. |
| [LIT-375](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-375.md) v2 | Structural Learning Theory: A Metric-Topology Factorization Approach | Li (2026), arXiv:2602.07974. >- The formal core of Xin Li's structural-learning programme. Width w(P; γ, δ) is the least number of open cells on each of which some predictor is γ-contractive with conditional risk ≤ δ. The paper proves that width is incomparable with the per-cell VC dimension (Thm 2.2). It shows that with K < w cells there is an n-independent error floor η(w, K), under a non-degeneracy assumption stated in the body (Thm 2.4, Assumption 2.3). Width is at least c·β₁·L/D₀ under a bounded-overlap assumption (Thm 2.5), and discovering all basins costs Ω(w log w) samples (Thm 2.6). The CS-Laplacian eigenvalue count converges uniformly to the predictor-relative count w_G(P) when n ≳ (H_G + d_X log(1/r_x) + log(1/δ′))/(r_x^{d_X} g_eff²) (Thm 3.5); no result shows that w_G equals width. There are no experiments. | Proposed — read in full 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-324](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-324.md)); >- Promising and unproven. It is the programme's fullest and most careful formal statement, and it carries the learning theory of [LIT-374](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-374.md) §3 with the assumptions in the body. Its routine results hold, and its bouquet slip is repairable. What would settle it: - a theorem that the CS count for a learned predictor equals w(P; γ, δ), not w_G(P); - a K-sweep on benchmarks of known width, showing the floor at K < w for routed learners, and testing whether a capacity-matched monolithic model shows it; - the decoupled-versus-joint training comparison it motivates but does not run. |
| [LIT-411](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-411.md) | Could a Large Language Model be Conscious? | Chalmers (2023), arXiv:2303.07103; Boston Review, 9 August 2023; from a NeurIPS 2022 invited talk. Asks for a feature X that LLMs have (or lack) and that indicates consciousness (or its absence). Self-report, seeming-conscious, conversation and general intelligence give at most weak evidence for it. Biology, senses and embodiment, world and self models, recurrent processing, a global workspace and unified agency are the evidence against. All but biology are temporary. On mainstream assumptions: under 10% credence for current LLMs, 25% or more for conscious LLM+ systems within a decade. Twelve challenges are offered as roadmap or red flags. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-345](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-345.md)), from arXiv v3 (the Boston Review text), with v1's conclusions compared; worth reading as the clearest short statement of the case for and against consciousness in LLMs, and as the origin of the "theory-balanced" credence approach that Butlin et al. built on. Its method is a regimented request for a feature X, and its verdicts are credences offered "for illustrative purposes": under 10% for current LLMs, 25% or more for conscious LLM+ systems within a decade, on "mainstream assumptions". It does not break the deadlock [THEORY-023](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-023.md) describes. It is an instance of it: mimicry undercuts self-report, the main obstacles are theory-derived, and biology is set aside rather than answered. |
| [LIT-427](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-427.md) | Pandemonium: A Paradigm for Learning | Selfridge (1959), Mechanisation of Thought Processes Vol. I (HMSO), pp. 513–526 plus discussion to p. 531. Pattern recognition by a "pandemonium": data demons hold the input, computational subdemons compute features, each cognitive demon "shrieks" a weighted sum of them, and a decision demon picks the loudest. The system learns by hill-climbing on the weights and by "natural selection" on the subdemons, culling those of low worth and breeding new ones by mutation and by "conjugation" of pairs. It is applied to telling dots from dashes in hand-keyed Morse. In the discussion McCarthy proposes reading the demons' private computation as unconscious and their public shouting as conscious thought. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-360](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-360.md)); worth reading as the first published architecture of a mind-like process built from many quasi-independent "demons", each doing one narrow job, with no part holding the whole's competence. That is the decomposition template that Minsky's agents inherit. Cite it as an engineering proposal with a preliminary result reported only in discussion, not as a theory of mind. Its one remark on consciousness is McCarthy's, in the discussion, and it is an aside. |
| [LIT-608](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-608.md) | Deep Equals Shallow for ReLU Networks in Kernel Regimes | Bietti & Bach (2021), ICLR 2021. Dot-product kernels on the sphere are diagonal in spherical harmonics, with one eigenvalue µ_k per degree k shared by N(d, k) ~ k^(d−2) harmonics. Theorem 1 reads the asymptotic decay of µ_k off the kernel function's expansion at ±1: a non-integer exponent ν there gives µ_k ~ k^(−d−2ν+1). The arc-cosine kernels have ν = 1/2 and 3/2, and composing them preserves ν, so the NTK of a deep ReLU network decays as k^(−d) and its random-feature kernel as k^(−d−2), exactly as for two layers. Deep and shallow ReLU kernels therefore have the same RKHS, the same as the Laplace kernel's for the NTK. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-475](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-475.md)): main text and Appendix A in full, the proofs in Appendices B and C followed at the level of their lemmas. Worth reading as the general rule behind the NTK eigenvalue decays the record holds: for a dot-product kernel on the sphere, the decay of its spherical-harmonic eigenvalues is fixed by the kernel function's non-integer exponent at the endpoints ±1 (Theorem 1). Deep ReLU kernels keep the shallow exponent, so depth leaves the spectrum's shape unchanged: µ_k ~ C(d, L) k^(−d) for the NTK and k^(−d−2) for the random-feature kernel, with only the constant growing in L (Corollaries 2–3). |
| [LIT-611](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-611.md) | Gemma Scope: Open Sparse Autoencoders Everywhere All At Once on Gemma 2 | Lieberum et al. (2024), Google DeepMind technical report. Gemma Scope releases JumpReLU sparse autoencoders trained on the attention, MLP and residual-stream activations of every layer of Gemma 2 2B and 9B, and of three layers of 27B: over 400 SAEs, over 2,000 counting sparsity variants, and over 30 million latents. Each latent fires only above a learned threshold θ_i, and training penalises the L0 count of active latents directly, through straight-through estimators. Evaluation is by sparsity–fidelity curves (delta LM loss and FVU against mean L0). Base-model SAEs transfer to the instruction-tuned model, wider SAEs split latents, and the authors state that no agreed metric of SAE quality exists. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-482](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-482.md)). Worth reading as the technical report for the open SAE suite that later SAE studies, including the anthology's, are run on, and as the clearest statement of what a JumpReLU SAE is. A JumpReLU SAE is a learned hard threshold per latent, z ⊙ H(z − θ), trained against squared reconstruction error plus λ‖f(x)‖₀ (Eqs. 3–4). The report releases over 400 such SAEs (over 2,000 counting the sparsity variants) on every layer and sublayer of Gemma 2 2B and 9B and on three layers of 27B. Its evaluations are sparsity–fidelity curves, with no criterion offered for choosing a width or a sparsity; the authors say there is no consensus on what measures SAE quality. |
| [LIT-612](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-612.md) | The Convergence Rate of Neural Networks for Learned Functions of Different Frequencies | Basri, Jacobs, Kasten & Kritchman (2019), NeurIPS 2019. In the linearised dynamics of a wide two-layer ReLU network, on uniform data on a sphere, the Gram matrix H∞ is a convolution, so its eigenvectors are Fourier modes or spherical harmonics. Its eigenvalues are computed in closed form per frequency. Without bias, every odd frequency k ≥ 3 has eigenvalue zero, so the network cannot represent or learn it (Theorems 2 and 4). With a zero-initialised bias all frequencies pass. The eigenvalues fall as 1/k² on S¹ and, numerically, about 1/k^(d+1) on S^d, so the time to learn frequency k grows as k² and k³ on the circle and the 2-sphere. Deep and residual networks show the same exponents. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-481](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-481.md)): main text in full, the supplementary derivations of the S^d eigenvalues skimmed. Worth reading for the closed-form NTK eigenvalues per frequency and the exact null space they reveal. On the circle the bias-free two-layer ReLU kernel has eigenvalue 2(k²+1)/(π²(k²−1)²) on even k ≥ 2 and exactly zero on odd k ≥ 3 (Eq. 12), so such a network cannot represent cos 3θ at all (Theorems 2 and 4). A zero-initialised bias fills the null space, with 1/(π²k²) on odd k (Eq. 13). Convergence time then grows as k² on S¹ and about k³ on S², and shallow, deep and residual networks match: fitted exponents 1.93–2.15 on S¹ and 2.74–3.13 on S² (Figs. 6–7). |
| [LIT-613](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-613.md) | Traces of Class/Cross-Class Structure Pervade Deep Learning Spectra | Papyan (2020), JMLR 21(252). Cross-entropy indexes every deepnet quantity by example, class and would-be class, a two-way MANOVA layout. In the spectra of features, backpropagated errors, gradients, the Fisher, the Hessian and weights, knockouts attribute the top outlier to the global mean, C−1 outliers to between-class second moment, a mini-bulk of C(C−1) to between-cross-class covariance, and the main bulk to within-cross-class covariance. Feature and error class means separate from the bulk and become orthogonal with depth. Gradient class means are approximately feature class means ⊗ error class means, layer by layer; K-FAC's single Kronecker product misaligns the Fisher's outliers and the class-wise CFAC aligns them. For multinomial logistic regression on a Gaussian class model the expected Fisher spectrum is derived exactly. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-474](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-474.md)); worth reading as the general account of class/cross-class structure in deepnet spectra: features, backpropagated errors, gradients, Fisher, Hessian and weights all show one outlier from the global mean, C−1 from class means, a mini-bulk of about C(C−1) from cross-class means, and a main bulk from within-class variation. Per layer, gradient class means are approximately Kronecker products of feature class means and error class means, which is why K-FAC, pairing every class with every class, misaligns the Fisher's outliers, and CFAC, pairing each class with itself, aligns them. Proved only for multinomial logistic regression on a Gaussian model. |
| [LIT-618](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-618.md) | Prevalence of Neural Collapse during the terminal phase of deep learning training | Papyan, Han & Donoho (2020), PNAS 117(40). Training past zero error (the terminal phase, TPT) drives four linked phenomena in the last layer: within-class variability collapses (Tr(Σ_WΣ_B†)/C → 0), centred class means become equinorm and equiangular with cosines −1/(C−1), a simplex ETF; classifier rows become proportional to the means; and the decision becomes nearest class mean. Measured on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-10/100, STL10 and ImageNet with VGG, ResNet and DenseNet, 480 models. Test accuracy and DeepFool robustness keep improving during TPT. Theorems: NC1–NC2 imply NC3–NC4 for the Webb–Lowe and Soudry max-margin classifiers, and the simplex ETF uniquely maximizes the small-noise error exponent. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-476](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-476.md)); worth reading as the source of neural collapse: in the terminal phase of training, last-layer features collapse to their class means (NC1), the centred means form a simplex equiangular tight frame (NC2), the classifier aligns with them (NC3) and the decision becomes nearest class centre (NC4). Measured on 7 datasets × 3 architectures; NC1–NC2 imply NC3–NC4 for the Webb–Lowe and max-margin classifiers, and the simplex ETF is the unique optimal codebook in a vanishing-noise Gaussian channel. It explains Papyan's Hessian outliers as class means outgrowing collapsing within-class variation. |
| [LIT-624](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-624.md) | Towards Understanding the Spectral Bias of Deep Learning | Cao, Fang, Wu, Zhou & Gu (2019). For a two-layer ReLU network trained by gradient descent on squared loss, the training residual projected onto the eigenfunctions of the NTK integral operator with the r_k largest eigenvalues decays like (1 − λ_(r_k))^T (Theorem 4.2). This holds for any labelling, provided the sample size beats the eigengap and the width is polynomial in λ_(r_k)^(−1). On uniform data on S^d the eigenfunctions are spherical harmonics, with µ_k = Ω(k^(−d−1)) for k ≫ d and Ω(d^(−k+1)) for d ≫ k on even degrees, and µ_k = 0 on odd k ≥ 3 (Theorem 4.3). Lower degrees are learned first, faster, and with fewer samples and narrower networks. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-483](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-483.md)): main text and Appendix A in full, the proofs in Appendix B followed at the level of their lemmas. Worth reading as the theorem that makes "spectral bias" a statement about NTK eigendirections: for a two-layer ReLU network trained by gradient descent, the residual projected onto the top r_k eigenfunctions of the NTK integral operator shrinks like (1 − λ_(r_k))^T (Theorem 4.2), for any target, with sample size governed by the eigengap λ_(r_k) − λ_(r_k+1). On uniform spherical data the eigenfunctions are spherical harmonics, the odd degrees above 1 have eigenvalue zero, and µ_k = Ω(max(k^(−d−1), d^(−k+1))) for even k (Theorem 4.3). |
| [LIT-657](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-657.md) | The Generalization Ridge: Information Flow in Natural Language Generation | Chang, Deng & Chen (2025), COLM 2026. InfoRidge estimates, layer by layer and through fine-tuning, the matrix-based mutual information between a transformer's last-token hidden state and the embedding of the target token, and between each block's residual update and that target. In GPT-2 Small and Medium, Qwen-2.5 0.5B and Llama 3.1 8B on CLUTRR, ECQA and a synthetic arithmetic task, it rises, peaks in the upper-middle layers and falls. On the synthetic task the peak coincides with the best OOD early-exit accuracy while ID accuracy keeps rising. Middle blocks add the most information, attention to task tokens peaks there, and residual scales fitted on OOD data downweight the last layers. The profile persists over 50 decoding steps on CNN/DailyMail. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-536](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-536.md)); worth reading as a layer-wise information profile of fine-tuned language models: a matrix-based Rényi estimate of I(Zℓ; Y), between the last-token hidden state at layer ℓ and the input embedding of the true next token, rises through the early layers, peaks in the upper-middle layers and falls in the last few, the "generalization ridge". On a synthetic arithmetic task with GPT-2 Small the peak (0.27 at layer 10 of 12) is where OOD early-exit accuracy is best (56.9%) while ID accuracy keeps rising to 93.2% at layer 12. Learned residual scales put less weight on the final layers when fitted on OOD data. The estimator is a kernel-alignment quantity, not Shannon mutual information: at layer 12 it falls to 0.019, near its layer-6 value, where the same layer decodes the target with 93% ID accuracy. |
| [LIT-665](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-665.md) | ZipIt! Merging Models from Different Tasks without Training | Stoica, Bolya, Bjorner, Ramesh, Hearn & Hoffman (2023), ICLR 2024. Merging differently initialised models trained on disjoint tasks fails under permutation, because the permuted model sits in a basin for its own task and not the other's. ZipIt! instead merges correlated features within and across models through merge and unmerge matrices, and can stop merging part-way, giving a shared trunk with task heads. The abstract reports a 20–60% improvement over prior work on CIFAR and ImageNet splits; it comes near the ensemble with partial zipping, and proves a tighter LMC barrier bound than Entezari et al. when units are redundant. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-523](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-523.md)), main text and Appendices A–F, the proof in Appendix G followed to its reduction to Entezari et al.; worth reading as the case that permutation is the wrong symmetry for merging models trained on different tasks. ZipIt! matches features by activation correlation within each model as well as across the two, and can stop merging at a chosen layer, leaving a multi-head model. On disjoint halves of CIFAR-10 it reaches 79.1% joint accuracy where Git Re-Basin reaches 46.2%, and partial zipping comes within a few points of the ensemble. Its theorem tightens Entezari et al.'s barrier bound when a model has redundant units. With full merging on ImageNet-1k it is no better than a permutation baseline (8.6%), so the gains there come from leaving later layers unmerged. |
| [LIT-667](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-667.md) | Does Data Scaling Lead to Visual Compositional Generalization? | Uselis, Dittadi & Oh (2025), ICML 2025. Two labelled concepts with n values each form an n × n grid; training shows k combinations per value and testing uses the rest. On dSprites, 3DShapes, PUG, colored MNIST and a new FSprites, ResNet-50s trained from scratch reach near 100% on seen pairs and fall sharply on unseen ones; 4× more in-distribution data does not close the gap, while more values and more combinations do. Features pass from spurious, to discriminative but entangled, to linearly factored and near-orthogonal as combinatorial coverage grows. Exact linear factorization makes k = 2 sufficient for perfect generalization. Frozen DINO, DINOv2 and CLIP features are above chance but far from that ideal. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-525](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-525.md)); worth reading as a controlled test of whether more data buys visual compositional generalization: in an (n, k) grid where each of n values of two concepts is seen in only k combinations, ResNet-50s trained from scratch fail on unseen pairs whatever the data volume (4× more in-distribution data leaves 60–80% drops), and succeed only as the fraction of combinations seen rises, when their features become linearly factored (a pair's embedding is the sum of per-concept vectors; R² > 0.8). Under exact linear factorization, k = 2 combinations per value suffice for a linear classifier to get all unseen pairs right (Proposition 4.1). DINO, DINOv2 and CLIP features are partly factored. Model selection is oracle, on the test set, by design. |
| [LIT-669](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-669.md) | Mechanistic Mode Connectivity | Lubana, Bigelow, Dick, Krueger & Tanaka (2022), ICML 2023. Two models are mechanistically similar if they are invariant to the same interventions on the data-generating process. Models that use a spurious cue and models that ignore it are mode connected along quadratic paths but not along linear ones, even after permutation matching, and the paper conjectures that a linear barrier implies mechanistic dissimilarity. For a one-hidden-layer ReLU network it proves only the converse: mechanisms of different complexity cannot be linearly connected. Naive fine-tuning on clean data stays linearly connected to the pretrained model and keeps its reliance on the cue; a fine-tune that forces a barrier removes it. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-538](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-538.md)); worth reading as the paper that ties a loss barrier to a difference in what two models compute. It defines two models as mechanistically similar when they are invariant to the same interventions on the data-generating process, finds that models relying on a spurious cue and models ignoring it are connected by quadratic paths but not by linear ones, even after permutation, and conjectures that a linear barrier always signals mechanistic dissimilarity. The conjecture is proved only for a one-hidden-layer ReLU network on a synthetic process; the evidence is synthetic cues on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Dominoes. |
| [LIT-674](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-674.md) | Going Beyond Linear Mode Connectivity: The Layerwise Linear Feature Connectivity | Zhou, Yang, Yang, Yan & Hu (2023), NeurIPS 2023. When two trained networks are linearly mode connected, whether by spawning from a shared early checkpoint or by permutation alignment, the features of nearly every layer of the weight-interpolated network are proportional to the interpolation of the two networks' features (LLFC). LLFC on the output layer implies LMC. Weak additivity of ReLU and a commutativity condition between layers' weights and features together imply LLFC, and Git Re-Basin's two matching objectives are each one factor of the commutativity residual. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-512](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-512.md)); worth reading as the finding that linear mode connectivity reaches inside the network: whenever two trained networks are linearly connected, by spawning or by permutation, the feature map of almost every layer of the interpolated network points in the direction of the interpolated feature maps (LLFC). Two conditions, weak additivity of ReLU on the two networks' pre-activations and a commutativity of each layer's weights with the other network's features, imply exact LLFC (Theorem 1), and Git Re-Basin's weight and activation matching each minimise one factor of the commutativity residual. Image classification only. |
| [LIT-678](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-678.md) | Intermediate Layer Classifiers for OOD generalization | Uselis & Oh (2025), ICLR 2025. Linear probes on the frozen features of an intermediate layer (ILCs) are compared with last-layer retraining for out-of-distribution classification on CMNIST, Waterbirds, CelebA, MultiCelebA, CIFAR-10C, CIFAR-100C and ImageNet variants, with ResNets and ViTs. Few-shot (probe trained on OOD data), the best intermediate layer usually wins, by more when OOD data are scarce. Zero-shot (probe trained on ID data, OOD only for selecting the layer), it beats retraining the last layer, sharply under subpopulation shift. Layer L − 2 beats L − 1 in every dataset shown. A distance-ratio sensitivity score finds intermediate features less displaced by the shift than penultimate ones, most of all for minority groups. | Active — read 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-541](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-541.md)); worth reading as the measurement that, under distribution shift, a trained classifier's best linear probe is usually not on the penultimate layer: Intermediate Layer Classifiers (linear probes on frozen layer-l features, l ≤ L − 2) beat last-layer retraining in the few-shot setting on most of nine shifted datasets, and, trained only on in-distribution data, raise worst-group accuracy from 79.4% to 87.1% on Waterbirds and 56.0% to 82.0% on CelebA. The proposed reason is that penultimate features move further under shift, especially for minority groups, while intermediate ones stay put. Selection of the layer uses OOD validation data, and the gains for ViTs are small. |
| [LIT-792](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-792.md) | Transformers learn in-context by gradient descent | von Oswald, Niklasson, Randazzo, Sacramento, Mordvintsev, Zhmoginov and Vladymyrov (2022), ICML 2023. Proposition 1 constructs weights for which one linear self-attention layer transforms each token (x_j, y_j) to (x_j, y_j − ΔW x_j), with ΔW one gradient step on the context's squared loss, so the query token's read-out equals the prediction of the updated linear model. A trained single layer matches the construction up to scale; deeper models outperform K steps of gradient descent and match GD++, gradient descent on inputs transformed by I − γXXᵀ. Synthetic regression only. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-621](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-621.md)); worth reading here for one exact identity: with constructed key, query, value and projection matrices, one linear self-attention layer applied to tokens (x_j, y_j) changes every token exactly as one gradient-descent step on the context's squared regression loss would change the targets (Proposition 1), so reading a context and updating an implicit model's weights on it produce the same prediction. A trained single layer finds those weights up to scale; deeper trained models match a preconditioned variant (GD++) rather than plain gradient descent. Everything is on synthetic regression with small attention-only models. |
| [LIT-796](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-796.md) | The Surprising Effectiveness of Test-Time Training for Few-Shot Learning | Akyürek, Damani, Zweiger, Qiu, Guo, Pari, Kim and Andreas (2024), ICML 2025. Training on leave-one-out in-context tasks beats training on the bare pairs. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-637](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-637.md)); worth reading here as a controlled comparison of two uses of the same demonstrations: held as context (in-context learning) or turned into a temporary update of the model's weights (test-time training, per-task LoRA, discarded after the task). With nothing added but the update, BIG-Bench Hard 10-shot accuracy goes from 50.5% to 57.8% and fine-tuned ARC accuracy roughly sixfold on an 80-task subset (5% to 29%). The update works best when its training data keep the in-context format. The comparison is empirical, at 1B–8B parameters, on two benchmarks with known leakage risk. |
| [LIT-801](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-801.md) | Learning to (Learn at Test Time): RNNs with Expressive Hidden States | Sun, Li, Dalal, Xu, Vikram, Zhang, Dubois, Chen, Wang, Koyejo, Hashimoto and Guestrin (2024), ICML 2025. Makes a sequence layer's hidden state the weights W of an inner model f, updated per token by a gradient step on a learned self-supervised reconstruction loss, with output f(θ_Q x_t; W_t). With a linear f and batch gradient descent this is exactly linear attention (Theorem 1); with the Nadaraya–Watson estimator as inner learner it is exactly softmax self-attention (Theorem 2). TTT-Linear and TTT-MLP match or beat Mamba at 125M–1.3B and keep lowering perplexity to 32k tokens of context, where Mamba plateaus after 16k. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-620](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-620.md)); worth reading for its reframing of a sequence layer as a learner trained on its own context: the hidden state is the weights of an inner model, the update rule a gradient step on a self-supervised loss, the output rule the inner model's prediction. Two exact identities follow: a linear inner model with batch gradient descent is linear attention (Theorem 1), and the Nadaraya–Watson estimator as inner learner is softmax self-attention (Theorem 2). The empirical part, TTT-Linear and TTT-MLP against Mamba and a Transformer at 125M–1.3B, is an architecture result that belongs to the anthology's question. |
| [LIT-814](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-814.md) | Rethinking the Role of Demonstrations: What Makes In-Context Learning Work? | Min, Lyu, Holtzman, Artetxe, Lewis, Hajishirzi and Zettlemoyer (2022), EMNLP 2022. What the demonstrations do supply is the input distribution, the label space and the input-label pairing as a format; keeping the format with only inputs or only labels retains up to 95% of the gain. Meta-training for in-context learning sharpens the effect. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-607](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-607.md)); worth reading as the measurement that separates what a demonstration supplies from whether its labels are right: across 12 model–method pairs up to GPT-3 and 26 classification and multi-choice datasets, replacing gold labels with random ones costs 0–5 points, while removing the input distribution, the label space or the paired format costs much more.
